title: Two Systems, One Number
context: Grade 4, late in the chapter. An adult sees two charts being compared. What the page is actually doing is showing that a number and the way a number is written are two different things, and it does it by holding the digits still and moving only the commas.

writeup.why: Find out how one number can be written two different ways, and why both of them are correct.
writeup.look: A row of digits with a chart above it and another below, each with its own headings and its own commas.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Two Systems, One Number' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many commas have been laid against how many the chart wants, two numbers side by side in ink, the first climbing as each tile drops; on the third phase it carries the periods read so far against the periods in the number, and on the fourth the amount being converted, in lakh and in million, one under the other. Nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. A control column 180 wide runs down the left of the working area at x 64: the system switch 180 by 56 at 64,214, a two ended rocker reading Indian at one end and international at the other; lay the commas 180 by 56 at 64,286; read it out 180 by 56 at 64,358; the opening page preset 180 by 56 at 64,430; and the conversion strip 180 by 220 at 64,502, two rows of paired plates with an equals bar between them, one lakh against one hundred thousand on the upper row and ten lakh against one million on the lower. The chart block is 875 wide at x 270, seven columns of 125 that every layer shares. The Indian chart is 875 by 160 at 270,202: a period strip 56 tall along its top carrying three named bands, lakhs over two columns, thousands over two and ones over three, and under it a heading row 104 tall of seven ruled cells, ten lakhs, lakhs, ten thousands, thousands, hundreds, tens and ones. The digit row is 875 by 132 at 270,370, seven cards 108 by 132 each centred in its column, the digits in ink, with the period bands drawn behind them at the full 132: deep blue for the ones period, green for the thousands, vermilion for the lakhs and rose for the millions when the lower chart is the one being read. The comma rail runs under the row at 270,506, 875 by 40, with two comma tiles 20 by 40 riding on it; a tile slides along the rail from gap to gap and never crosses a card, and where a reading wants one comma fewer the spare slides off the right hand end and waits there in grey. The reading strip is 875 by 36 at 270,550 and fills one period at a time, in words, as the read control works along the row. The international chart is 875 by 140 at 270,590, the Indian one turned over: a heading row 84 tall of seven cells, millions, hundred thousands, ten thousands, thousands, hundreds, tens and ones, with its period strip 56 tall along the foot naming millions over three columns, thousands over three and ones over three. The two charts are the same columns in the same places, so one digit card sits in a column of the chart above and a column of the chart below at the same time. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across with a thirteenth key that lays a comma, on the first three phases, so a child writing an answer writes its commas as part of it; on the fourth it is a choice pad of large word keys, one lakh, ten lakh, one hundred thousand, one million, ninety lakh and nine million, which are the words the conversion strip holds. On the third phase a word strip of the four period names, ones, thousands, lakhs and millions, sits under the keys, because a reading is given there in words. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the ones period is deep blue, the thousands period green, the lakhs period vermilion and the millions period rose; whatever settles the answer on this stage is amber; a zero that is only holding a place open is grey; and chrome never borrows one of them, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
writeup.finish: The card shows one number written both ways, with the period names under each, and the opening page figure converted.

phases.win: the commas sit at the Indian boundaries and the three bands are named
phases.does: lays the commas in from the right and names each period
phases.goal: the Indian system groups three places, then two, then two
phases.says: Count three from the right, then two, then two. Where did the commas land?
phases.check: Away from the screen: write any seven digit number and say where the two commas go, and which end you counted from.
phases.feels: the commas are counted in, and the counting starts at the end you do not read from
phases.hands: Write the seven digits once, large, with a finger width between them, and let the child count three in from the right hand end and press a pencil into that gap, then two more, then two more, saying the count out loud.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which end did you count from? Second rung, the phase's: how many places are in the first group? Third rung: the row is cut to five cards and the child lays a single comma into it. The pad stays open behind all three.

wrong.why: the first comma came after three, and a pattern that opens in threes ought to go on in threes.
wrong.move: lays the second comma three gaps along from the first, carrying the grouping on in threes.
wrong.screen: both comma tiles slide back to the right hand end of the rail and the counting runs again from the right, one card lifting per count: three cards lift and the first tile drops into the gap behind them, then two cards lift and the second tile drops behind those. The gap the child chose stays outlined and hollow on the rail, and their answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: reading and writing both begin at the left, so counting a number begins there too.
wrong.move: counts in from the left, so the commas land after the first three digits and the next two.
wrong.screen: a small ink figure appears under each card in turn from the right hand end, and the gap the count reaches lights before any tile moves; the count then runs again from the left and stops without lighting anything, because the chart is read from the other end. Nothing the child laid is taken away.

phases.screen: a row of seven digits with the Indian chart lit above it
phases.soWhat: The Indian chart groups the places three, then two, then two, counted in from the right.
phases.concept: The Indian chart groups two, two and three

phases.win: the commas rest at every third place and the digit row is unchanged
phases.does: watches the commas slide and checks that no digit has moved
phases.goal: the digits do not move, only the commas do
phases.says: Watch the digits, not the commas. Did any of them move?
phases.check: The same digits written two ways. Is one of those two numbers bigger than the other?
phases.feels: everything about the number changes except the number
phases.hands: Write the digits once on a long strip and rule two lines under the strip, one for each system's commas, so one row of digits carries both readings at the same time and neither has to be rewritten.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: has any digit left its place? Second rung, the phase's: which group does the leftmost digit belong to in each chart? Third rung: the switch is thrown slowly, one comma tile at a time, with an ink ring held round the digit row throughout. The pad stays open.

wrong.why: five million sounds like a bigger thing than fifty-six lakh, and the words are the part a child hears.
wrong.move: says the number has grown, because it now reads five million and a moment ago it read fifty-six lakh.
wrong.screen: every card draws a thin ink line up into its column in the chart above and down into its column in the chart below, seven lines each way, and each line lands in a column standing for the same amount under either name, ten lakhs above and millions below. The two readings are then printed one above the other with the unchanged digit row between them.

wrong.why: with the commas moved the end group looks short, and a number that does not fill its groups looks unfinished.
wrong.move: slides a digit card along to make the last group come out full.
wrong.screen: the card lifts, is carried back to the place it came from and set down, its own column lighting as it lands, while under it the two comma tiles run freely along their rail. The rail is drawn under the row and never through it, so the commas are the thing that moves and the cards are the thing that does not.

phases.screen: the same row of digits with the switch thrown to international
phases.soWhat: Only the grouping moves. Two sets of commas can sit under one row of digits and neither is wrong.
phases.concept: The international chart groups three, three and three

phases.win: the spoken reading and the printed reading match
phases.does: reads each period aloud and adds its name, then checks against the printed line
phases.goal: a number is read one period at a time, not digit by digit
phases.says: Read the first chunk, then say its name. Now the next chunk.
phases.check: Read this number to me. How many chunks did you say, and which chunk had no name after it?
phases.feels: a long number stops being a string of digits and turns into three short numbers with names
phases.hands: Cover all but one group of a written number with two fingers, read out loud what is showing and then say that group's name, and walk the fingers along to the next group.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many digits are in the chunk you are reading? Second rung, the phase's: what does the chart call that chunk? Third rung: one band is lit and the rest of the row is dimmed, so a single chunk is read on its own before the next is lit. The pad and the period words stay open.

wrong.why: every number met so far has been short enough to read as its digits, and digits are what is on the row.
wrong.move: reads the number out one digit at a time, naming each digit in turn instead of each period.
wrong.screen: the period bands come forward behind the digits and the cards of one band lift together as a single chunk; the reading strip fills a chunk at a time, the digits of the period first and then its name, and a chunk already read stays printed while the next one lifts. The child's reading stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the other two periods are named as they are read, so the third looks as though it ought to be named as well.
wrong.move: says the name of the ones period too, finishing the reading with the word ones.
wrong.screen: the strip prints the whole reading with the word ones on the end, then that one word thins out of the strip while the three digits of the period stay lit; the ones heading on the chart stays exactly where it is, because the period keeps its name and only goes unsaid.

phases.screen: a six digit number with its period bands showing
phases.soWhat: A number is read one period at a time, each followed by its name, and the ones period keeps its name unspoken.
phases.concept: Each period is read with its own name

phases.win: the opening question is answered and the strip agrees with the chart
phases.does: converts the library figure from one system to the other
phases.goal: ten lakh and one million are two names for one amount
phases.says: Ten lakh make one million. So how many lakh is that library?
phases.check: Nine million books, or ninety lakh books. Is that two libraries or one?
phases.feels: a question left open on the very first page closes fifteen pages later
phases.hands: Write one lakh and one hundred thousand on two cards and ten lakh and one million on two more, lay them face up in a row, and have the child pair them off before anybody says which is which.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many lakh make one million? Second rung, the phase's: how many of those does the library hold? Third rung: the strip is cut to its lower row alone, ten lakh against one million, and the child counts that row out for each million. The word keys stay open.

wrong.why: both words name the big period at the left hand end, and one of them is the only one the chapter has used until now.
wrong.move: answers nine lakh for the library, taking one million for one lakh.
wrong.screen: the conversion strip fills in, one lakh drawing out against one hundred thousand on the upper row and ten lakh against one million on the lower, each pair of plates sliding together until they are exactly the same length. Nine of the lower plates are then laid end to end and counted along in tens of lakh. The child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: they sit in one sentence on one page, and a page usually keeps to one way of writing things.
wrong.move: says both numbers on the opening page are written in the same system.
wrong.screen: the opening page line comes up with its figures and each is lit in turn over the charts: the students number carries its comma in a gap that both charts agree about, and the library number carries a period name that only the chart below has, and that chart's millions band lights as the word is read. Nothing the child wrote is removed.

phases.screen: the conversion strip beside the numbers from the chapter opening
phases.soWhat: Ten lakh and one million are two names for one amount, so one library can be counted in either.
phases.concept: One lakh, one million, and the numbers from the first page

writeup.delight: The second phase, the first time the switch is thrown. The seven digit cards each take a thin ink ring and hold absolutely still, and everything else on the stage moves at once: the two comma tiles run along their rail to new gaps, the vermilion lakhs band behind the digits draws in by a column and turns rose as it becomes a millions band, the green thousands band widens by the column the lakhs band gave up, and the heading row above the digits hands its names over to the heading row below. When it settles the rings lift and the digits are exactly where they were. Nothing else moves and the voice says nothing while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a row of seven digit cards stands across the middle of the working area with the Indian chart drawn above it, its seven place headings filled and its period strip empty, and the comma rail under the row holding its two comma tiles parked at the right hand end. On the second the international chart below is drawn in as well and the switch beside the row is set to Indian with the commas already laid. On the third a six digit number stands in the row with its period bands showing behind the digits and the reading strip under it empty. On the fourth the conversion strip is open in the control column and the figures from the chapter's opening page are already in the row. The running count at the top left is empty and the slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the first comma tile on its rail, or the system switch, or the leftmost period band, gives one slow pulse while the voice says there are the same digits and two charts. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any number as far as seven digits, the switch free, and both charts on screen together. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on regrouping, reading and converting between the two systems.
voiceLines: The same digits, and two charts. Lay the commas in from the right.
Count three from the right, then two, then two. Where did the commas land?
Watch the digits, not the commas. Did any of them move?
Read the first chunk, then say its name. Now the next chunk.
Ten lakh make one million. So how many lakh is that library?
The same digits. Look at where the commas sit now.
Free play. Any number, either chart, and the switch is yours.
Slide the commas back and count in from the right again.
One number written two ways, and both of them right.

observations.why: Only the grouping changed, and a group is not a place.
observations.soWhat: A number and the way a number is written are two different things.
observations.observe: The seven digit cards stood in the same seven places under both sets of commas.

observations.why: The Indian chart counts three, then two, then two; the international counts three, three and three.
observations.soWhat: Where a comma goes is a rule of the system, not a fact about the number.
observations.observe: Both charts wanted two commas in this number, and not one gap was shared.

observations.why: They are one amount with two names, one name from each system.
observations.soWhat: I can swap the name without swapping the amount.
observations.observe: One lakh and one hundred thousand filled the conversion strip to exactly the same length.

observations.why: Ten lakh make one million, so nine million is nine tens of lakh.
observations.soWhat: The question the first page asked about those numbers has an answer, and this is it.
observations.observe: The library of nine million books came back as ninety lakh books.

serves.exercise: identifying the systems of numeration used in the numbers on the opening page
returning to the history of the university and answering the related question

source_tool.description: One row of digits sits in the middle of the stage and two charts are stacked around it, the Indian above and the international below, each with its own period headings. A switch moves the reading between them. Flipping it slides the commas along the row to their new boundaries and re-colours the period bands, two and two and three for the Indian chart and three and three and three for the international, while the digits themselves visibly stay exactly where they are. A read control speaks and prints the number one period at a time, saying each period name after its digits and skipping the name of the ones period. A conversion strip along the side keeps one lakh against one hundred thousand and ten lakh against one million. The last phase loads the numbers printed on the chapter's opening page, which is where the question asked there is finally answered.
source_tool.art_direction: One row of digits between two charts / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.
Drawn things, not abstract boxes: token tiles, place value charts with ruled columns, a number line with labelled ticks, digit cards that can be picked up, and lettered tiles for the Roman numerals.

A large number is always shown with its digits sitting in named places, with the period bands behind them and the commas drawn where the Indian system puts them. A bare numeral with no chart behind it is never used to teach place value.
Where tokens or blocks stand for a quantity, exactly the stated number of them is drawn and they stay countable at a glance and never overlap.
A place is told apart by its column label first and by its band colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a token or a place the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. The ones period is deep blue, the thousands period is green and the lakhs period is vermilion, and those three bands are the same three colours in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The millions period is rose and appears only where the international chart does. A digit under discussion, or the digit that decides a comparison, is amber. A zero holding an empty place open is grey, because it is a placeholder and not a quantity. All of that holds in greyscale, because a period is told apart by its band and its label before its colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Slide the commas back and count in from the right again.
voice.onNext: The same digits. Look at where the commas sit now.
voice.opening: The same digits, and two charts. Lay the commas in from the right.
voice.onFinish: One number written two ways, and both of them right.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any number, either chart, and the switch is yours.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: The Indian chart groups two, two and three
The international chart groups three, three and three
Each period is read with its own name
One lakh, one million, and the numbers from the first page

placement.where: After the Indian chart is secure and a number from a newspaper has been found with commas in the wrong places. The tool holds the digits still while the commas move, which paper cannot.

answer_key.rule: The Indian system groups the places three, then two, then two, so the periods are ones, thousands and lakhs. The international system groups them three, three and three, so the periods are ones, thousands and millions. The digits never move between the two. A number is read one period at a time, each followed by its name except the ones period. One lakh is one hundred thousands and ten lakh is one million.
answer_key.wrong: The commas are slid back to the start and laid in again one at a time, counted out from the right. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Count three digits in from the right and write the first comma.
Count two more digits and write the second comma.
What is left at the left hand end is the lakhs period.
items.answer: 56,87,709, grouped as two, then two, then three
items.question: Put Indian commas into 5687709 and say how the digits are grouped.
items.checkpoint: The Indian system groups three places, then two, then two.
items.misconception: Placing a comma after every three digits all the way along.

steps: Count three digits in from the right and write a comma.
Count three more and write another comma.
Check the digit row: not one of them has moved.
items.question: Put international commas into the very same digits, 5687709.
items.checkpoint: The same digits regroup without any of them changing place.
items.misconception: Believing the number itself has changed because it now looks different.

steps: Read the digits of the leftmost period together, then say its name.
Fifty-six, then lakh. Eighty-seven, then thousand.
The ones period has no name, so simply say seven hundred nine.
items.answer: Fifty-six lakh eighty-seven thousand seven hundred nine
items.question: Read 56,87,709 aloud in the Indian system.
items.checkpoint: Each period is read as a chunk followed by its name, except the ones.
items.misconception: Reading the number out digit by digit instead of period by period.

steps: So nine million is nine groups of ten lakh.
Nine times ten lakh is ninety lakh.
items.question: A library holds 9 million books. How many lakh is that?
items.checkpoint: Ten lakh and one million are two names for one amount.
items.misconception: Treating one million as one lakh and answering nine lakh.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Rewrite 325047 in the Indian place value chart with its commas.
Rewrite 752368 in the Indian system and write it in words.
items.final_answer: 7,52,368, seven lakh fifty-two thousand three hundred sixty-eight

items.question: Rewrite 652104 in the international place value chart with its commas.
Rewrite 963258 in the international system and write it in words.
items.final_answer: 963,258, nine hundred sixty-three thousand two hundred fifty-eight

items.question: Write two hundred four thousand six hundred one in numerals.
Write seven hundred thousand four hundred seven in numerals.
How many thousands make one lakh?
The opening page gives ten thousand students and nine million books. Which of those uses an international period name?
items.final_answer: Nine million, because million is an international period. In the Indian system that is ninety lakh

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

teaching_notes: Write the digits once and put two sets of commas underneath the same row, on paper, before opening the tool. Then let the tool do it, because watching the commas slide while the digits hold still is the thing the page is claiming and paper has to redraw. Say one lakh and one hundred thousand in the same breath until they stop sounding like two different amounts. Go back to the opening page in the last phase; the question asked there was left open on purpose fifteen pages earlier and this is where it closes.
generation_prompt: Build a numeration comparison tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. One row of up to seven digits sits centrally, with an Indian place value chart above it and an international one below, each carrying its own period headings. A system switch moves the active reading between them: flipping it animates the commas sliding along the row to their new boundaries and recolours the period bands, three then two then two for the Indian chart and three then three then three for the international, while the digits remain visibly fixed in place. A lay the commas control counts in from the right and places each comma in turn. A read it out control prints and speaks the number one period at a time, appending each period name and omitting the name of the ones period. A conversion strip holds one lakh against one hundred thousand and ten lakh against one million. A preset loads the figures printed on the chapter's opening page. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Lay the commas into the row of digits, then throw the switch and watch them move. Check that no digit moved with them. Read the number out one chunk at a time, and say the name of each chunk.
